description: AI-VAPT is an autonomous AI-driven Vulnerability Assessment & Penetration Testing framework combining traditional VAPT with neural intelligence. It automates recon, scanning, and reporting using AI-powered analysis, CVE mapping, and exploit prediction — built for ethical hackers and enterprise security teams.

summary.one_liner: AI-VAPT is a TypeScript framework, described as an autonomous AI-driven vulnerability assessment and penetration testing tool, that aims to automate reconnaissance, scanning, CVE mapping and reporting.
summary.what_it_does: The README describes a layered design: an AI layer for exploit prediction, CVE correlation and anomaly detection; a recon layer for subdomain, DNS, port, directory and service enumeration; a vulnerability layer for CVE mapping, version fingerprinting and misconfiguration detection; an exploitation layer for controlled, safe-mode payload validation; and a reporting layer that produces PDF/HTML reports with severity ranking and remediation paths. It lists integrations with tools such as Amass, Subfinder, Nmap, Shodan API, CRT.sh, Nikto, Dirsearch, Wapiti, BurpSuite API, Exploit-DB and Metasploit. The README also lists scan types (web, network, API, cloud, IoT) and a planned LLM reasoning engine, exploit chain visualization, OSINT enrichment and cloud audits as roadmap items. The README does not document how these pieces are wired together or which are fully implemented.
how_to_run: node -v && npm -v  (verify Node.js and npm are installed)
notable: Layered architecture separating AI analysis, recon, vulnerability mapping, safe-mode exploitation and reporting
Reporting engine that outputs PDF/HTML reports with severity ranking and remediation guidance
Claims a privacy-by-design mode with no stored data and an offline-capable operation mode
Modular design for plugging in new scanners, ML models or third-party tools
Supports periodic testing pipelines via CI/CD integration
caveats: Many features (ML exploit prediction, LLM reasoning, OSINT enrichment, cloud agents) are described in marketing-style text or the roadmap, and the README does not show their implementation status
Setup steps only cover installing and starting a dev server; the README does not explain how to run actual scans or configure the integrated tools
Offensive tooling (exploitation, Metasploit, token dumping) requires authorization; the README gives no licensing or legal-use guidance beyond calling it ethical hacking
